item.title: When Did We Stop Sitting Together?
item.description:
Loneliness

When Did We Stop Sitting Together?

Personal Perspective: We are connected more than ever, but are we really together?

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Loneliness may involve not only being alone but also a lack of genuine presence when we are together.
  • Informal gathering places and unstructured time create opportunities for meaningful human connection.
  • Relearning how to sit, listen, and stay with one another may help restore a sense of belonging.

I can’t pinpoint exactly when it happened. There was no announcement. No cultural agreement that we should spend less time simply being with one another. I don’t remember a specific day when we collectively decided that sitting together was no longer important. Yet, somewhere along the way, something changed.

I remember when people sat around the kitchen table long after dinner was over. The plates were still there. The coffee had gone cold. Someone would inevitably tell a story we had already heard at least a dozen times. Nobody seemed particularly concerned about leaving. We just sat.

Sometimes the conversations were important. Most of the time, they weren’t. Someone complained about work. Someone talked about a neighbor. People argued about something insignificant and then moved on to another subject without ever resolving the first one. Occasionally, nobody said anything at all. But we stayed.

Today, silence seems to make us uncomfortable. When a conversation slows for even a few seconds, someone reaches for a phone. I have done it. Most of us probably have. We scroll through social media, check an email that could easily wait, or respond to a notification that somehow feels more urgent than the person sitting directly in front of us.

We have become remarkably connected while many of us feel increasingly alone.

Perhaps loneliness is about being physically alone. Maybe part of our loneliness comes from how rarely we are fully present when we are together.

Being Near Someone Is Not the Same as Being With Them

Friends
Source: Helena Lopez / Unsplash

Human beings have a deep desire to be seen, heard, and understood. Humanistic psychology has long emphasized the importance of genuine human relationships. Carl Rogers wrote about empathy, authenticity, and the value of creating relationships in which people feel accepted and understood.

We often discuss these ideas within the context of therapy. But empathy and presence do not belong exclusively in a therapist's office. Being present with another person does not require a clinical intervention. Sometimes it simply requires a chair.

I have noticed this most often when I cook. I enjoy grilling and smoking meat, which is an admittedly slow hobby. A brisket does not care about my schedule. It cannot be rushed because I have somewhere else to be. Sometimes it takes 12 hours. Sometimes 16. Occasionally, it seems determined to take as long as humanly possible. But something interesting happens when food takes that long to cook. People sit down.

Someone wanders outside and asks when the food will be ready. I usually give an estimate that turns out to be completely wrong. Eventually, someone pulls up a chair. Then someone else joins.

At first, everyone checks their phones. Then, gradually, the phones seem to disappear. Someone asks a question. A story starts. Another person remembers something related and interrupts with a story of their own. Before long, people are talking.

Nothing extraordinary has happened. Nobody announced that we were going to spend the afternoon strengthening our interpersonal relationships. Nobody said, “I am feeling lonely and would benefit from meaningful social interaction.” They simply asked, “You got another chair?”

Maybe that is how human connection has always worked.

Have We Made Connection Too Complicated?

Time together
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

We often talk about loneliness as though it requires an elaborate solution. We download apps designed to help us connect. We attend organized events. We schedule social activities weeks in advance. There is value in intentional connection, particularly for people experiencing isolation. But I sometimes wonder whether we have made ordinary human connection more complicated than it needs to be.

For generations, gathering was simply part of living. Families ate together. Neighbors sat on porches. Friends stopped by. People spent time in diners, barbershops, libraries, parks, and other places where conversation could happen without being the official purpose of the visit.

Social scientists sometimes refer to these informal gathering spaces as “third places”—places outside home and work where people can regularly encounter one another. The important word may be informal. Connection didn’t always require an appointment.

Today, many of us move quickly from one responsibility to another. Work follows us home through email. Entertainment is instantly available. Our phones offer an endless stream of information competing for our attention. In that environment, sitting around can feel unproductive. Perhaps that is part of the problem.

Human connection is not always productive. Conversations wander. People repeat themselves. There are awkward pauses. Sometimes we spend two hours talking and cannot remember exactly what we discussed the next day. Yet, something happened during those two hours. We were together.

Maybe We Need to Learn How to Stay Again

Come Together
Source: Shane Rounce / Unsplash

From a humanistic perspective, there is profound value in simply being present with another person. We do not always need to fix them. We do not need to analyze their behavior, offer advice, or search for the perfect response. Sometimes another person simply needs to experience our presence. There is a difference between hearing someone and listening to them. There is also a difference between being near someone and being with them.

Technology is not the enemy. I use my phone far more than I probably should. Technology allows us to maintain relationships across great distances and connect with people we might never otherwise meet. But connection at a distance should not make us invisible to the person sitting three feet away. Maybe we need to become comfortable with sitting again.

Leave the plates on the table for another 20 minutes. Let the coffee get cold. Sit on the porch. Pull a chair next to the smoker, even if the person cooking has absolutely no idea when the brisket will be finished. Ask someone a question and wait long enough to hear the entire answer.

And when there is a moment of silence, perhaps we do not need to immediately fill it or escape from it. Maybe silence between people who are comfortable with one another is not an absence of connection. Maybe it is evidence of it.

We spend a great deal of time searching for solutions to loneliness, disconnection, and the growing sense that people no longer understand one another. These are complex problems. They will not be solved by a single conversation around a kitchen table.

But perhaps the kitchen table is not a bad place to begin. I still do not know exactly when we stopped sitting together. Maybe the more important question is when we will start again. There is probably an empty chair somewhere nearby. Pull it up. And stay awhile.

item.title: My Children Recovered From Mental Illness—Then I Did, Too
item.description:
PANDAS

My Children Recovered From Mental Illness—Then I Did, Too

Personal Perspective: Witnessing my children's rapid recovery changed my life.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • We can revolutionize how we treat mental illness by using medical and mental health interventions.
  • Immune mediated conditions, such as PANS/PANDAS, offer a road map for healing.

Things we can’t explain or understand, we often separate. Mental illness is no different.

In Europe, people started separating those with mental illness from those with medical illness in the Middle Ages, believing they had demonic possession; by the 1700s, many countries had “lunatic asylums,” where those with mental illness could be treated in isolation. Today, we've reached the point where we have separate systems, billing practices, and diagnostic manuals for each.

Growing up in a family that passed down mental illness the way others did cancer, I accepted this separation. My family members understood that some of us would inherit the “mental illness gene.” Unlike cancer, there would be no cure. Medication, therapy, and grit would manage symptoms for the rest of the unlucky person’s life.

When my children were diagnosed with an immune-mediated condition, this separation dissolved. Their healing, and mine following theirs, illuminated a bridge connecting the two systems and revealing another path—one offering relief from suffering and true healing.

Mental Health Is Medical

Both of my children presented with a myriad of mental health issues in early childhood: obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), eating restriction, ADHD, sensory issues, irrational fears, panic attacks, rage, mood liability, even suicidality,

For six years, I used every tool in my personal and professional mental health toolbox to help them stabilize, yet their symptoms only increased in severity. I began to worry I might lose one to suicide.

Another mother mentioned a condition I knew nothing about: PANS/PANDAS (pediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome/pediatric autoimmune disorder associated with strep). These are illnesses triggered by infection (e.g., strep throat, pneumonia, flu) or non-infectious (e.g., environmental, metabolic) factors, causing the onset of mental health symptoms.

I was skeptical. As a social worker, I had been trained to rule out medical causes of mental health, per the DSM-5-TR, but not this. Out of desperation, I had them evaluated.

Both children met the clinical criteria for PANS/PANDAS. Within two weeks of treatment (antibiotics and anti-inflammatories), we saw signs of profound healing. Their suicidality abated, their OCD relented, their sensory issues calmed—in ways I had never experienced personally or professionally.

How "Family Genes" Can Lead a Diagnosis Astray

I was a Division 1 swimmer, part of a team that just finished second at the NCAA Championships, when my mental health sharply declined. Professionals, confused by this sudden deterioration, tried to talk me out of it. “You have so much to live for," they said. "You have to stop this”—as if self-harm, an eating disorder, and depression were a choice any All-American athlete would make.

When willing myself into health didn’t work, multiple diagnoses were proposed; ultimately, my family history led to a bipolar II diagnosis. I didn’t fit the diagnostic criteria perfectly. My faulty "family genes" offered a logical explanation, albeit one that meant a life of symptom management.

Twenty years later, when my children were diagnosed with PANS/PANDAS, I learned more about OCD, including how often it is misdiagnosed. With sudden clarity, I recalled the intrusive, looping thoughts that began for me in early childhood. I was so ashamed of them; I created rituals, obsessively apologized, and sought reassurance to manage my fear.

Three pronged approach to PANS/PANDAS Treatment
Source: Swedo SE, Frankovich J, Murphy TK. Overview of Treatment of Pediatric Acute-Onset Neuropsychiatric Syndrome. J Child Adolesc Psychopharmacol. 2017 Sep;27(7):562-565. doi: 10.1089 Epub 2017 Jul 19. PMID: 28722464; PMCID: PMC5610386.

In college, those thoughts became louder, screaming with self-hatred and suicidal ideation, no longer easily quieted. Running parallel were physical issues: an inability to sleep, chronic infections, and stomach issues.

My bipolar II diagnosis didn’t fit just right because it wasn’t right. I had OCD. I thought about the illnesses that had precipitated my acute decline in college and wondered: Could I have what my children had?

Mental and Physical Illness Can Be Both/And, Not Just Either/Or

Watching my children heal, I dared to wonder if I could as well. Treatment for PANDAS/PANS is a “three-pronged” approach: address the medical causes (which includes both removing the inflammatory source(s) and regulating the immune system) and treat the mental health symptoms.

In PANS/PANDAS, the infectious (or non-infectious) trigger in the body causes inflammation in the brain—specifically the basal ganglia, where OCD is believed to originate. When treatment is successful, mental health symptoms abate as the immune system and inflammation in the body are managed.

This inflamed basal ganglia, however, sits just above the amygdala (our body’s fear center), triggering a near perpetual fight/flight/freeze response. The brain is constantly telling the body, “There is a lion chasing me.” Previously not-scary events (school, sports, friends) can become terrifying.

When the amygdala is activated, the body/brain remembers the trigger to avoid future harm. After medical interventions calm the immune system and reduce inflammation, the brain must be retrained for safety. Therapeutic interventions (i.e., cognitive behavioral therapy, exposure response prevention) are commonly used to support.

Retraining the brain becomes essential when you also learn that the cascade of stress hormones generated by the amygdala creates an inflammatory and immune dysregulating impact on the body. The discovery that PANS/PANDAS offered a road map for how the body and the brain communicate with one another felt revolutionary, suggesting the DSM 5-TR medical rule-out may be more aptly termed a medical "rule-in.”

Everyone Deserves a Chance to Heal

With so much time passed, now an adult, I would never know what my trigger was. I learned that other illnesses—thyroiditis, Lyme, autoimmune conditions (i.e., lupus, multiple sclerosis)—can also present as psychiatric. I decided to seek out medical interventions and the correct treatment for OCD anyway.

Brain Injury in PANS/PANDAS
Source: Zheng J, Frankovich J, McKenna ES, et al. Association of Pediatric Acute-Onset Neuropsychiatric Syndrome With Microstructural Differences in Brain Regions Detected via Diffusion-Weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging. JAMA Netw Open. 2020;3(5):e204063. doi:10.1001

I expected nothing to change, believing my mental illness was “who I was.” Then inexplicably, the intrusive thoughts and crippling anxiety stopped. The brain fog, stomach issues, and sleep improved. I felt like I was waking up from deep sleep—regaining parts of myself I never knew existed.

With profound gratitude for our healing, I share this information as often and with as many people as I can. We introduced the three-pronged approach at the therapeutic school I oversee. Students previously terrified to attend school are now attending daily. Students who used to spend months in psychiatric hospitals have yet to return to one. Students who never thought they would live to see their 18th birthday are now in college.

This qualitative, if anecdotal, data—from student after student who appeared “treatment resistant” but is now healing—is to me clear evidence that we need medical and mental health interventions to heal.

Mental health and medical health are not meant to be divided. The time to change hearts and minds is now, to transform our perspective and practices. We all deserve healing.

item.title: Four Practical Steps to Soothe Anxious Sensations
item.description:
Anxiety

Four Practical Steps to Soothe Anxious Sensations

What to do when the internal storm of anxiety rages.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Instead of fighting anxious sensations, try viewing them as an objective observer.
  • Shift from trying to silence sensations to asking what they are trying to communicate.
  • Real healing comes from offering your frightened nervous system a steady, kind, patient presence.
Source: Ann Tarazevich/Pexels

One of the most common questions I get in my anxiety relief courses is, “How do I get rid of anxious sensations as quickly as possible?”

This is a completely understandable question. When panic and anxiety show up, they don’t just stay in our thoughts, they tend to take over our physiology too. And it's unpleasant, to say the least. When the body feels like it’s in danger, it makes complete sense to desperately want to escape the discomfort.

This is one of the hardest parts of working with anxiety. The body is screaming “Danger!” while your mind is pleading, “Make these feelings go away.”

Of course, we don’t have to pretend to like anxious sensations. But difficulty arises when we hold the belief that the sensations must go away before we can be okay, or when we mistakenly believe that focusing on them or hating them will actually help to relieve them. When we get hyper-focused on the unpleasant sensations, it seems like that's all that exists. This creates a feedback loop where fear fuels sensations, and sensations fuel more fear.

To break this cycle, we don’t need to try to force the fear to leave. We need to change how we respond to it. Here are four practical shifts to help you navigate the internal storm of anxious sensations.

1. Widen Your Awareness

When anxious sensations appear, the brain’s natural survival mechanism is to zoom in on the perceived threat. The mind tends to hyper-focus on whatever is most uncomfortable in the body.

One way to shift this pattern is to experiment with widening your awareness. Take a moment to scan your body for areas that feel neutral. Maybe your feet feel neutral, or your hands, your shoulders, or even one toe. See what it’s like to shift your focus from unpleasant sensations to areas of your body that feel neutral.

You can also look around your physical environment. Notice the colors or shapes around you. Feel the surface supporting your body. Remind your nervous system: “Even though my body is highly activated right now, in reality, I am safe in this moment.” These neutral observations provide your brain with evidence that you are actually safe.

2. Shift From Fear to Curiosity

I like to think of intense physical sensations as internal weather patterns. Most of us don’t tend to judge a thunderstorm outside or sit and watch it all day and assume the sun will never shine again. We simply accept that a storm is passing through. Our sensations are like that too.

Instead of meeting an internal storm with disapproval ("I hate this. How can I get rid of these feelings?"), try meeting it as a curious observer.

Try shifting your inner dialogue to: "That’s interesting. My mouth feels dry. There’s some fluttering in my belly. I can observe these sensations as if they were weather patterns.”

Curiosity shifts the brain and body into a different mode than fear. It changes your role from being consumed by sensations to being an objective observer of them. This shift often softens the struggle, even if the sensations don't disappear immediately.

3. Listen to the Message

Our bodies tend to whisper when they need something. If we ignore the whisper, they get louder. If we continue to ignore them, they eventually have to scream.

Healing often begins when we shift from asking, "How do I make this stop?" to asking, "If these sensations could speak, what would they say?"

When we stop dreading anxious sensations and actually listen, they often hold profound clues about what needs attention, expression, or support in our lives.

One of my clients realized her panic was pointing to a lack of healthy boundaries. Her body flared up with panicky sensations whenever she gave more of herself than she actually had to give.

A student of mine discovered that symptoms of anxiety were reactions to years of relentless self-criticisms that the body could no longer take.

Another student realized her panic was screaming for a true pause. She needed to build in more moments of fulfilling rest.

Ultimately, anxious sensations are not an enemy to defeat. They are either old tensions waiting to be processed, or current indicators guiding you toward what needs attention or change.

4. Parent Your Frightened Nervous System

If a terrified child ran to you for comfort, I highly doubt you would yell at them to, “Stop being afraid!” or “Calm down already!” You would likely offer them your calm, steady, loving presence. You might wrap them in a hug, rock them gently, and reassure them that you are here, they are safe, and this will pass.

Your nervous system responds to that same kind of care. Instead of trying to overpower anxiety, try to soothe it. Put a hand on your heart. Wrap yourself in a warm blanket. Take a few slow breaths. Speak to yourself with the tenderness you would offer someone you love.

If you try these tools and the sensations of anxiety or panic persist or come right back, please know that you’re not doing anything wrong.

Many people interpret the return of anxiety or panic as a failure to cope with life. But rewiring the nervous system doesn’t happen because internal storms never return. It happens because, moment by moment, your brain accumulates evidence that you are safe and that you can ride the storms out with supportive practices.

Progress doesn’t mean you never feel anxious again. It’s about meeting the moment differently, and regularly asking yourself: Can I become just a little less afraid of being afraid? Can I promise not to abandon myself while this storm of sensation moves through my system?

Real healing doesn’t come from trying to force fear out the door. It comes from showing your brain, over and over again, that when internal storms arrive, you will meet yourself with curiosity, compassion, and patience. Over time, your brain realizes it no longer needs to sound the alarm quite so loudly because you’re processing your emotions, challenging unhelpful thoughts, setting healthy boundaries, and actively listening to your needs.

item.title: How to Navigate Recovery in Schizophrenia
item.description:
Psychiatry

How to Navigate Recovery in Schizophrenia

Personal Perspective: The difficult and unpredictable journey of recovery.

Posted July 8, 2026

Source: open_arms_initiative / Pixabay

In April of 2007, I left a psychiatric hospital knowing that I would always need an antipsychotic medication to maintain stability. But as I resolved to stay in treatment, I did not realize what a difficult and unpredictable new journey I was embarking upon.

I would need to find a provider who would really listen and want to partner with me. I needed a convenient pharmacy to dispense my meds and reliable transportation to doctors’ appointments and other crucial appointments. Additionally, I would need to complete extensive paperwork to access services such as Medicaid, Supplemental Security Income (SSI), and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). At the time, I could not have envisioned the time and effort it would take to establish a solid and reliable path to recovery.

Once these details were set in place, I could resume chasing my dreams and look forward to a bright future again.

Keeping appointments

Sometimes in schizophrenia, a person is initially offered a wide and diverse treatment team, which can give the person their best chance of stability and help them thrive. In other instances, a treatment team must be built over time from various sources identified by the patient. A doctor or psychiatric nurse practitioner is fundamental for prescribing medication, and a good clinician will do whatever it takes to convince a person with psychosis to always take their medications as prescribed and engage in treatment. Often, a psychiatrist or nurse practitioner will also offer talk therapy and support, and even friendship.

In addition to a prescribing clinician, sometimes a person with schizophrenia will work with a counselor and or a psychologist for talk therapy. Others may benefit from a case manager.

As these appointments are being set up, it is imperative to keep a calendar, carefully track appointment times, and manage transportation. People who don’t drive should arrange help from a family member or friend in advance. Others may use their local bus system. If someone is taking the bus, they should practice in advance, traveling to the place where the appointment will later be held to get comfortable knowing where they need to go.

For those on Medicaid, at least in Ohio, free transportation to and from appointments can be arranged. Personally, I have used the free transportation provided by Medicaid on occasion to visit my dentist.

Labs and Meds

Some people who struggle with schizophrenia or other psychoses need regular lab work. About a year after I consented to treatment, I began the medication clozapine, which required a weekly blood test for six months. Fortunately, a lab was a long walk from my parents’ home, where I was living at the time, though my parents were kind enough to give me rides so I did not have to walk. I usually saw the same phlebotomist, and as the weeks went by, we told each other about our lives and became friends. Sometimes, getting a blood test or a long-acting injectable provides an opportunity for deepening relationships.

In addition to getting lab work done, I also had to diligently pick up my meds every month. Fortunately, at first, my pharmacy was also close to my parents’ house, and the pharmacy staff members were helpful. Today, I know everyone in my pharmacy by name, and I enjoy having the opportunity to see them when I get my medications.

Finding a prescriber

In my experience, finding a clinician was a very difficult challenge. I felt my first doctor did not listen to me, understand me, or have the initiative to really get to know me. He seemed to be treating my schizophrenia, but not me as an individual. However, he did me a great service by prescribing a medication that would greatly improve my life.

Fortunately, a year following my diagnosis, I was referred to a professor at the University of Cincinnati School of Medicine, Henry Nasrallah, who listened to me and tried to understand my experience. He also found out about my history in depth and knew about my college scholarship, the research I had done before my illness began, and my experience performing violin in orchestras and for a recording company. He wanted to get me back to that life.

A relationship with a clinician should go both ways. A patient should have a way to get hold of the provider quickly if needed. The clinician must see the patient as a person with hopes, dreams, and a history. Nasrallah gave me a phone number where I could connect quickly, if needed. At that point, it was up to me to be respectful of his time and not call unless my need was urgent. When I met him in 2008, I immediately felt a sense of connection. In my case, this connection was so strong that we would later establish a nonprofit organization together in 2016.

Paperwork for social services

Today, in 2026, having been in sustained recovery for 18 years, I do not need many of the services and the support I did in the beginning, such as Social Security income. But applying and being approved for Supplemental Security Income (SSI) was part of my journey to independence. Fortunately, following my diagnosis and while I was still very ill, my dad filled out most of the paperwork to apply for Medicaid, food stamps (SNAP benefits), and SSI.

SSI, Medicaid, and SNAP personnel have always worked with me dependably. There have been a few mistakes in my paperwork over the years, and our Cincinnati Legal Aid office has fixed these errors for me every time, always quickly and pro bono.

Managing schizophrenia is hard enough, but it doesn’t end there. One must be diligent about appointments, labs, getting meds, and completing complicated legal paperwork. But it is worth it. Once these habits are set in place, the prospect of solid and sustained recovery becomes increasingly possible.

item.title: Why Adult Friendships Keep Failing
item.description:
Friends

Why Adult Friendships Keep Failing

Adult friendship is hard, but there is a better way.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • We need to know the difference between party friends, context friends, and our secure base friends.
  • Secure base friendships are characterized as: available, responsive, reciprocal, and repairable.
  • Proper framing helps us not resent the friends that disappoint us, because we understand them better.

When someone says it’s hard to make friends in adulthood, we tend to believe them. What comes next is a focus on making friends through advice such as “get out there more,” “initiate,” “try new things.” These recommendations help adults get exposure to people who could be their friends. After this, we need to start asking the question: Are we making the right friends?

A lot of clients I work with sigh when considering the effort it takes to find and make new friends, because they tell me: What if I put in all this effort and it doesn’t work out? This is a real problem and reality that causes friend-making burnout and has an impact on our growing isolation.

And it makes sense that if we are going out there and expecting every new person we meet to be best friend material, we will burn out and be disappointed because not everyone fits that bill — but we don’t need them to be. Research shows that we humans actually have limits to how many friends we can have, and that number shrinks when it comes to the close friends that I call our "secure base" friends (more on that below).

Friendship is inherently ambiguous. There are no clear-cut rules for success or failure, like there are for more "established" relationship dynamics like romantic or familial bonds. But just because friendship is ambiguous doesn't mean we can't better educate and equip ourselves for success, and adapt ways to make friendship less mysterious.

You see, when we lack a complete view of friendship foundations, what can happen is we get ourselves out there, we invest time, energy, and emotion, but we invest it in the wrong places, and friendship frustration ensues.

This is why I often hear these common friendship problems in my office: I got ghosted. My friendship is one-sided. I’m always reaching out but never the one getting reached out to. I have a friend conflict that I don’t know how to handle, so I’m just going to walk away.

article continues after advertisement

I want to introduce the idea that while friendship is critical to human connection, knowing the kinds of friendship we are engaging in (and how to respect them) is vital to solving the confusion. More than that, having better friendship literacy and ways to practically apply improved friendship maintenance behaviors can do wonders for our generation.

Aristotle gives us a helpful archetype of friendship categories in his Nicomachean Ethics. The first is friendships of pleasure, the second is friendships of utility, and the third is true serious friends.

I’ve taken a slight liberty in renaming this a bit: We have party friends, context friends, and then our secure base friends.

Learning how to recognize these friendships gives us something profound. It gives us guideposts for relationships that are naturally ambiguous and how to respond (not react) when these ambiguous relationships start acting ambiguously! (Usually, our tendency is to ghost here, but there is so much more we can do).

So when a friendship feels off, we can assess it through educated eyes and ears: Maybe I’m expecting something different here than what they are willing or able to give?

When we have our secure base friends, we have available, reciprocal, and repairable friends.

When we have party and context friends: we have a rich network of people that make up the tapestry of our community net that adds fun, connectivity, and whimsy to our lives.

We need both, but primarily, when seeking friends, we need to prioritize our secure base friends (both making them and maintaining them with care and intentionality — which includes repair!), because it is there that close relational intimacy exists. And guess where we develop our secure base friends? From those friendships that start out as context or party friends! This isn't an either/or dynamic; it's a "yes – and" dynamic. Our context friends and party friends have the potential to become secure base friendships, yet we need to be aware of when that is or isn't happening, so that we can manage expectations appropriately.

By having all kinds of friends, we don’t resent the friends that disappoint us, because we understand them better.

A framework that helps us view our friendships appropriately is valuable for maintaining connection in a complex social landscape. Additionally, having a solid secure base of friendship with 3-5 close others gives a person the emotional security, support, and safety to get through the gauntlet that is adult life.

article continues after advertisement

This idea frees us up. We can feel we have no need for revenge, because we are radically accepting the reality that not every friend is a bestie, but friend-adjacent peers have solid places in our lives as well. And if we know what we’re working with, we can trust that our precious time, energy, and feelings are not wasted or neglected, but going to provide a valuable return on our investment.

In my new book Friendless: Why Adult Friendships Keep Failing, I discuss this and more. It will be published by the American Counseling Association in the Spring of 2027, and available wherever books are sold.

If you have any questions or a friend-frustrated story, I'd love to hear about it, so please reach out or follow me on Instagram @friendlessbook.

item.title: Beheading the Hydra and the Hidden Source of Symptoms
item.description:
Anxiety

Beheading the Hydra and the Hidden Source of Symptoms

When symptom-focused psychotherapy isn't enough.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Symptom substitution is a real though difficult-to-measure phenomenon in some cases.
  • Symptoms can have deeper psychological significance or meaning.
  • Suppressing symptoms makes it more difficult to discern their potentially helpful message.
Hercules and the Hydra of Lerna
Source: Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Wikimedia Commons.

One example of symptom substitution relates to what we have discovered about the effective treatment of substance abuse and addiction, in which the addictive behavior itself is seen today as the primary problem, as opposed to a symptom of another issue, and is directly addressed during treatment. But I would argue that while this may be the most pragmatic and efficacious treatment approach for substance use disorders, this does not preclude the possibility that the addictive behavior is driven or motivated by underlying emotional or psychological issues such as anxiety or depression, which, when unresolved or unaddressed, can lead to relapse from sobriety or to the formation of sundry psychiatric symptoms such as anxiety, depression, rage attacks, or other compulsive behaviors like workaholism, gambling, or compulsive sex, among others. There are reasons that addicts do what they do that underlie and perpetuate the symptoms of substance abuse itself.

Symptom Substitution Can Manifest in Personality Disorders

Treatment of so-called personality disorders—chronic, rigid, and pervasive patterns of distressing, destructive, or debilitating subjective experience and objective behaviors—excellently exemplifies this fascinating phenomenon insofar as the constellation of symptoms comprising, for instance, narcissistic (see my previous post), antisocial, or borderline personality disorder, are expressions of the underlying character structure which is itself, not unlike the Hydra, essentially unaffected by the targeted elimination or removal of one symptom (or regenerating head) in particular, despite our best efforts. Another example regards the treatment of anxiety. As is well-known in the medical and mental health field, anxiety, sometimes called the "great imitator," can take multifarious forms of somatic and psychological symptoms, from headaches, stomach problems, chronic pain or fatigue, insomnia, obsessive compulsive symptoms, phobias, panic attacks, and others. It stands to reason that if one anxiety symptom, say, engaging in some obsessive-compulsive ritual, is targeted and suppressed with therapy and or medication, another could conceivably crop up to take its place. Why? Though the specific symptom may be extinguished for now, the anxiety that it was defending against remains.

The nature of this underlying anxiety is another question. In psychoanalysis, it might be attributed to an unresolved Oedipal complex or other unconscious sexual conflict or repressed trauma. If, for instance, someone's anxiety symptoms are related to the repression or denial of some previous traumatic event, temporarily suppressing their anxiety will provide some immediate relief, but it does not address the repressed trauma in the same way that patiently exploring the possible significance or meaning of the anxiety might. And, what happens to the patient's motivation to do so once the initial anxiety symptom is ameliorated?

For existential psychotherapy, some anxiety is, well, more existential; it has to do with the existential facts of mortality (death anxiety), freedom (Kierkegaard called anxiety the "dizziness of freedom), responsibility, authenticity, integrity, and more. Indeed, for existential therapy, there is both normal or existential anxiety, which is not considered a psychiatric symptom requiring treatment but rather an inescapable experience of being human, and neurotic (or psychotic) anxiety, which is the consequence of chronically repressing, suppressing, or avoiding our existential anxiety. In this latter case, if the person's neurotic anxiety symptom is removed or alleviated without addressing the underlying existential anxiety that was being avoided, some other neurotic symptom can replace it.

Jungian Psychology and the Meaning of Symptoms

In Jung's analytical psychology, anxiety can accompany personal or archetypal contents of the unconscious becoming more conscious, or serve as a sign that, for example, we are not honoring our introverted or extraverted nature and, therefore, not in balance or harmony with ourselves. In any case, the point is that some psychotherapies see phenomena like anxiety not necessarily as pathological symptoms but as being potentially meaningful human experiences to which we must listen and from which we must learn. As Kierkegaard observed, anxiety can be our "best teacher." But if we hasten to deaden or dispel such symptoms as quickly as possible, we may be unwittingly forfeiting the opportunity to learn from them. And, if there is some vital lesson that needs to be learned about ourselves, and we choose to suppress or medicate our symptoms or metaphorical "demons," rather than tolerate and confront them, then might it not be possible that some new and different symptom will appear until we finally learn that lesson?

Finally, from the perspective of what I call "existential depth psychology," a unique synthesis of psychodynamic, Jungian, and existential therapy, symptoms are potentially helpful daimonic messengers from the unconscious trying to communicate something important about ourselves and how we are living our lives (see Diamond, 1996). Yes, psychiatric symptoms are typically painful, frightening, disturbing, distressing, uncomfortable, and sometimes debilitating. But without being so, they would never receive our attention. Symptoms are what bring someone into therapy. Of course, it is human nature to want to be rid of our agonizing symptoms as soon as possible. And, with some of today's psychotherapeutic techniques and psychiatric medications, this is more possible than ever before—at least temporarily. But is it truly always in our best interest to do so? If our symptoms are like Hydra heads, ultimately we cannot permanently defeat the fundamental life force—what I call the daimonic—that expresses itself through them if we only focus on symptoms.

Certainly, psychiatric symptoms can be not only excruciating but, like the mythological Hydra, toxic and dangerous, and sometimes they require some psychological or pharmacological suppression or mitigation. But even then, they can still be explored in therapy by asking: What might this symptom signify or mean? Why is this symptom happening to me right now? When did it start? What triggered it? What might it have to say about how my life is going? Or about what happened in the past? Or my concerns about what will happen in the future? (See Part 3.)

item.title: Why Well-Being Gets Lost in Autism
item.description:
Autism

Why Well-Being Gets Lost in Autism

New autism data reveals a striking gap between intentions and lived experience.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Well-being was ranked above communication, self-care, and academics.
  • Autistic adults report lower well-being than other autism community groups.
  • Many support systems prioritize well-being, but autistic individuals often don't feel it.
  • Measuring well-being is essential if we want it to become a meaningful outcome.

For years, conversations about autism support have focused on helping autistic individuals develop skills. We measure communication goals, academic achievement, daily living skills, and behavioral outcomes. These are important markers of growth. But a question has lingered beneath the surface: What if we're measuring many things that matter while overlooking what matters most?

A recent national survey commissioned by Proof Positive and conducted by Pathfinder Research sought to better understand well-being across the autism community. More than 1,000 autistic individuals, caregivers, educators, and service providers participated. The findings revealed overwhelming agreement on one point: well-being is essential.

Ninety-four percent of respondents said prioritizing the personal well-being of autistic individuals is either "very important" or "absolutely essential" within autism services and supports. No respondent described well-being as unimportant. That level of agreement is remarkable. Yet perhaps the most important finding was not the consensus itself. It was the disconnect hidden beneath it.

Most caregivers, educators, and service providers believe they are prioritizing well-being. In fact, 89 percent reported that well-being is a central focus or high priority in their work with autistic individuals. But when autistic individuals were asked the same question from their perspective, only 39 percent felt their support systems prioritized well-being to that same degree.

A similar pattern emerged when respondents were asked about time spent engaging in activities that support joy, meaning, purpose, and connection. Seventy percent of caregivers, educators, and providers reported spending significant time supporting well-being-focused activities. Only 24 percent of autistic individuals reported experiencing that level of engagement in their own lives.

article continues after advertisement

These findings raise an important question: When support systems believe they are prioritizing well-being, but the people receiving support do not experience it that way, what is being missed? The answer may be less about commitment to promoting well-being and more about implementing what produces well-being as an outcome.

The Challenge of Measuring Well-Being in Autism Services

What is measured gets attention. Schools track academic progress. Therapists monitor therapeutic goals. Healthcare providers collect clinical outcomes. Yet measuring well-being is rarely treated with the same level of rigor.

The survey found that only 6 percent of educators and service providers use a formal measurement tool to assess well-being. More than one-quarter reported not measuring well-being in any direct or indirect way. This creates a challenge. When well-being remains invisible, it becomes easy to assume it is improving because other forms of progress are occurring. But well-being is not automatically produced by skill acquisition.

A person can learn new skills and still feel disconnected. They can make academic gains while struggling emotionally. They can meet goals set by others without experiencing joy, a sense of purpose, or a sense of belonging. These outcomes matter because well-being is not merely an accompaniment to development. Increasingly, evidence suggests it may help drive development itself.

article continues after advertisement

For decades, autism services have often operated from an implicit assumption: build skills first and well-being will follow. The autism community appears to be telling us something different. Nearly seven in 10 survey respondents said improving well-being makes it easier to build other skills. Only 31 percent believed skill development should come first, and well-being would naturally follow. Autistic individuals endorsed this perspective most strongly.

This finding aligns with broader psychological research showing that people learn, grow, and adapt more effectively when they experience psychological safety, connection, positive emotion, and a sense of agency. Well-being and development are not competing priorities. They are deeply interconnected. When people feel understood and supported, learning becomes more accessible. Relationships become easier to navigate. Resilience grows. Motivation strengthens.

In this sense, well-being may be less of an outcome and more of a foundation.

The survey also revealed significant differences in well-being across the autism community. Autistic individuals reported the lowest levels of well-being, followed by caregivers. Educators and service providers reported substantially higher levels of well-being. This finding deserves attention.

Is the Autism Community Ready for a Shift in Priorities?

Caregivers often shoulder significant emotional, logistical, and financial demands. Autistic individuals frequently navigate systems that focus on challenges while overlooking strengths and quality of life. Both groups may experience stressors that directly affect well-being.

These results suggest that supporting autistic well-being cannot be separated from supporting the well-being of the people who care for and support autistic individuals. Well-being is relational. Flourishing rarely happens in isolation.

Perhaps the most encouraging finding from the survey is that the autism community appears ready for change. Well-being was consistently ranked as the number one priority above communication, self-care, socialization, and academics. Respondents overwhelmingly agreed that autistic individuals deserve lives characterized by joy, meaning, purpose, and connection.

The challenge now is translating agreement into action. That begins by listening carefully to autistic individuals and recognizing that good intentions do not always translate into lived experience. It means developing practical ways to assess and support well-being. It means treating well-being as a meaningful outcome rather than a hoped-for byproduct of other interventions.

article continues after advertisement

Most importantly, it means expanding our definition of success. For too long, autism support has largely been evaluated by what challenges are reduced or what skills are gained. Those outcomes matter. But they are not the whole story. Autistic individuals deserve more than support aimed at helping them survive. They deserve opportunities to flourish. The autism community has spoken clearly. The question now is whether our systems are prepared to listen.
